claim: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are multifunctional molecules found among all kingdoms of life that act as key components of the innate immune system of metazoans by modulating immune responses and defending against invading pathogens.
source: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are multifunctional molecules found among all kingdoms of life that act as key components of the innate immune system of metazoans by modulating immune responses and defending against invading pathogens (Zasloff, 2002a; Yeung et al., 2011; Mookherjee et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published works (Zasloff, 2002a; Yeung et al., 2011; Mookherjee et al., 2020).

claim: AMPs are potent antimicrobials with desirable pharmacodynamic properties and a low rate of resistance evolution.
source: AMPs are potent antimicrobials with desirable pharmacodynamic properties and a low rate of resistance evolution (Yu et al., 2018; Lazzaro et al., 2020; Spohn et al., 2019; Jangir et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published works (Yu et al., 2018; Lazzaro et al., 2020; Spohn et al., 2019; Jangir et al., 2021).

claim: There is widespread interest in the development of natural and synthetic AMPs for therapeutic use.
source: Given these benefits, there is widespread interest in the development of natural and synthetic AMPs for therapeutic use (Mookherjee et al., 2020; Hancock and Sahl, 2006; Magana et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published works (Mookherjee et al., 2020; Hancock and Sahl, 2006; Magana et al., 2020).

claim: The evolution of bacterial resistance to therapeutic AMPs may generate cross-resistance to host AMPs because they share common physicochemical properties and mechanisms of action.
source: However, a serious concern with the therapeutic use of AMPs is that they share common physicochemical properties and mechanisms of action with AMPs of host immune system, suggesting that the evolution of bacterial resistance to therapeutic AMPs may generate cross-resistance to host AMPs (Habets and Brockhurst, 2012; Kubicek-Sutherland et al., 2017; Fleitas and Franco, 2016; Andersson et al., 2016; Napier et al., 2013; Dobias et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to six published works (Habets and Brockhurst, 2012; Kubicek-Sutherland et al., 2017; Fleitas and Franco, 2016; Andersson et al., 2016; Napier et al., 2013; Dobias et al., 2017).

claim: Host AMPs play important roles in mediating bacterial colonization and fighting infection.
source: Given that host AMPs play important roles in mediating bacterial colonization and fighting infection (Salzman et al., 2010; Ostaff et al., 2013), cross-resistance to host AMPs could increase pathogen transmission and virulence (Groisman et al., 1992; Kidd et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Salzman et al., 2010; Ostaff et al., 2013).

claim: Cross-resistance to host AMPs could increase pathogen transmission and virulence.
source: Given that host AMPs play important roles in mediating bacterial colonization and fighting infection (Salzman et al., 2010; Ostaff et al., 2013), cross-resistance to host AMPs could increase pathogen transmission and virulence (Groisman et al., 1992; Kidd et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Groisman et al., 1992; Kidd et al., 2017).

claim: The evolution of resistance to antibiotics in many pathogens has been largely driven by the acquisition of resistance genes via horizontal gene transfer.
source: For example, the evolution of resistance to antibiotics in many pathogens has been largely driven by the acquisition of resistance genes via horizontal gene transfer (Partridge et al., 2018; MacLean and San Millan, 2019), but conventional experimental evolution approaches focus on variation that is generated by spontaneous mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Partridge et al., 2018; MacLean and San Millan, 2019).

claim: Colistin (polymyxin E) is an AMP produced by Bacillus polymyxa with similar physicochemical properties and mechanisms of action to metazoan AMPs.
source: Colistin (polymyxin E) is an AMP produced by Bacillus polymyxa with similar physicochemical properties and mechanisms of action to metazoan AMPs (Rodríguez-Rojas et al., 2015; Vaara, 1992; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Rodríguez-Rojas et al., 2015; Vaara, 1992) and a supplementary file.

claim: Colistin began to be used at a large scale in agriculture in the 1980s.
source: Colistin began to be used at a large scale in agriculture in the 1980s (Wang et al., 2017), but it is being increasingly used as a 'last-resort' antimicrobial to treat infections caused by multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative pathogens (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Colistin is being increasingly used as a 'last-resort' antimicrobial to treat infections caused by multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative pathogens.
source: Colistin began to be used at a large scale in agriculture in the 1980s (Wang et al., 2017), but it is being increasingly used as a 'last-resort' antimicrobial to treat infections caused by multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative pathogens (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2006.

claim: Colistin resistance has evolved in many pathogens.
source: Colistin resistance has evolved in many pathogens (Jochumsen et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2020; Snitkin et al., 2013), but the most concerning case of colistin resistance evolution comes from MCR genes in E. coli, as exemplified by mcr-1 (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published works (Jochumsen et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2020; Snitkin et al., 2013).

claim: E. coli acquired a composite transposon carrying mcr-1 in China at some point in the 2000s.
source: Phylogenetic analyses show that E. coli acquired a composite transposon carrying mcr-1 in China at some point in the 2000s (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: MCR initially spread in populations of E. coli from farms, where colistin was used as a growth promoter to increase the yield of chicken and pig production.
source: MCR initially spread in populations of E. coli from farms, where colistin was used as a growth promoter to increase the yield of chicken and pig production.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text without supporting data or citations in this sentence.

claim: mcr-1 became widely distributed across agricultural, human, and environmental sources due to the combined effects of bacterial migration and rapid horizontal transfer of mcr-1 between plasmid replicons and host strains of E. coli.
source: However, mcr-1 became widely distributed across agricultural, human, and environmental sources due to the combined effects of bacterial migration and rapid horizontal transfer of mcr-1 between plasmid replicons and host strains of E. coli (Wang et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published works (Wang et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2016).

claim: MCR-1 transfers phosphoethanolamine (pEtN) to lipid-A in the cell membrane, resulting in decreased net negative cell surface charge and thus lower affinity to positively charged colistin.
source: MCR-1 transfers phosphoethanolamine (pEtN) to lipid-A in the cell membrane, resulting in decreased net negative cell surface charge and thus lower affinity to positively charged colistin (Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2018.

claim: Loss of cell surface charge through membrane modification is a common resistance mechanism against cationic AMPs across bacteria.
source: Crucially, loss of cell surface charge through membrane modification is a common resistance mechanism against cationic AMPs across bacteria (Spohn et al., 2019; Andersson et al., 2016), suggesting that MCR-1 may provide cross-resistance to host AMPs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Spohn et al., 2019; Andersson et al., 2016).

claim: Membrane alterations produced by MCR-1 expression are associated with clear costs.
source: However, membrane alterations produced by MCR-1 expression are associated with clear costs (Yang et al., 2017), and it is equally possible that membrane remodeling could generate collateral sensitivity to AMPs, as has been observed with antibiotic resistance genes (Lázár et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: Membrane remodeling could generate collateral sensitivity to AMPs, as has been observed with antibiotic resistance genes.
source: However, membrane alterations produced by MCR-1 expression are associated with clear costs (Yang et al., 2017), and it is equally possible that membrane remodeling could generate collateral sensitivity to AMPs, as has been observed with antibiotic resistance genes (Lázár et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lázár et al., 2018.

claim: mcr-1 is usually carried on conjugative plasmids from a diversity of plasmid incompatibility types (such as IncX4, IncI2, IncHI2, and IncP1) that carry a large number of housekeeping and cargo genes.
source: mcr-1 is usually carried on conjugative plasmids from a diversity of plasmid incompatibility types (such as IncX4, IncI2, IncHI2, and IncP1) that carry a large number of housekeeping and cargo genes (Wang et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Wang et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2017).

claim: mcr-1 imposed a significant fitness burden in the absence of AMPs, reducing competitive ability by 3%.
source: Consistent with previous work (Yang et al., 2017), mcr-1 imposed a significant fitness burden in the absence of AMPs, reducing competitive ability by 3% (p=1.174e-15, two-sided Mann–Whitney U-test, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (p=1.174e-15, two-sided Mann–Whitney U-test) and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1, as well as a citation to previous work (Yang et al., 2017).

claim: mcr-1 provided a significant competitive fitness advantage at concentrations of host AMPs between ¼ and ½ of minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC).
source: However, mcr-1 provided a significant competitive fitness advantage at concentrations of host AMPs between ¼ and ½ of minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) (Figure 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The minimal selective concentration for colistin (¼ MIC) was only marginally lower than for host AMPs.
source: Although mcr-1 provided a greater fitness advantage in the presence of colistin as compared to host AMPs, the minimal selective concentration for colistin, ¼ MIC, was only marginally lower (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The sub-MICs required for the selection of mcr-1 overlap with the range of physiological concentration of host AMPs.
source: It is important to note that the sub-MICs required for the selection of mcr-1 overlap with the range of physiological concentration of host AMPs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and known physiological concentrations.

claim: The concentration of LL-37 required to select for MCR-1 (~3.4 μM) falls well within the reported physiological concentration range (up to 10 μM).
source: For example, the concentration of LL-37 required to select for MCR-1 (~3.4 μM) falls well within the reported physiological concentration range (up to 10 μM) (Barlow et al., 2010; Srakaew et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (~3.4 μM) and citations to two published works (Barlow et al., 2010; Srakaew et al., 2014) providing physiological concentration ranges.

claim: On average, MCR plasmids provided increased resistance to host AMPs by 62%.
source: On average, MCR plasmids provided increased resistance to host AMPs by 62% (mean fold change in MIC = 1.62; SEM = 0.11; t = 5.615; p<0.0001; Figure 2; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (mean fold change in MIC = 1.62; SEM = 0.11; t = 5.615; p<0.0001) and reference to Figure 2 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The average change in resistance conferred by MCR plasmids varied significantly between AMPs.
source: However, the average change in resistance conferred by MCR plasmids varied significantly between AMPs as MCR plasmids increased resistance to most AMPs, but generated collateral sensitivities to both PROPH and PR39 (Figure 2b; F8,40 = 7.85; p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (F8,40 = 7.85; p<0.0001) and reference to Figure 2b.

claim: MCR plasmids increased resistance to most AMPs, but generated collateral sensitivities to both PROPH and PR39.
source: However, the average change in resistance conferred by MCR plasmids varied significantly between AMPs as MCR plasmids increased resistance to most AMPs, but generated collateral sensitivities to both PROPH and PR39 (Figure 2b; F8,40 = 7.85; p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b (F8,40 = 7.85; p<0.0001).

claim: The AMP resistance profile of natural MCR plasmids was highly correlated with that of the synthetic pSEVA:MCR-1 expression vector (r2 = 0.845).
source: The AMP resistance profile of natural MCR plasmids was highly correlated with that of the synthetic pSEVA:MCR-1 expression vector, suggesting that changes in resistance observed in MCR plasmids were caused by MCR, and not by other genes present on these plasmids (r2 = 0.845; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (r2 = 0.845) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deletion of mcr-1 gene resulted in a wild-type level of resistance to AMPs.
source: As expected, deletion of mcr-1 gene resulted in a wild-type level of resistance to AMPs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The observed AMP resistance phenotype is largely due to the pleiotropic effects of MCR gene and is not distorted by other genes present on natural plasmids.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the observed AMP resistance phenotype is largely due to the pleiotropic effects of MCR gene and is not distorted by other genes present on natural plasmids.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing correlation between natural and synthetic MCR plasmids and deletion experiments.

claim: MCR generated large increases in resistance to colistin compared to host AMPs.
source: MCR generated large increases in resistance to colistin compared to host AMPs, supporting the idea that MCR genes are specialized for providing colistin resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing resistance levels.

claim: PROPH and PR39 have unique physicochemical properties, including high proline content.
source: These AMPs have unique physicochemical properties, including high proline content (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), which has been shown to be a common property of intracellular-targeting AMPs, as opposed to membrane-disrupting AMPs (Supplementary file 1; Scocchi et al., 2011; Gerstel et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and citations to published works (Scocchi et al., 2011; Gerstel et al., 2018).

claim: High proline content has been shown to be a common property of intracellular-targeting AMPs, as opposed to membrane-disrupting AMPs.
source: These AMPs have unique physicochemical properties, including high proline content (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), which has been shown to be a common property of intracellular-targeting AMPs, as opposed to membrane-disrupting AMPs (Supplementary file 1; Scocchi et al., 2011; Gerstel et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published works (Scocchi et al., 2011; Gerstel et al., 2018) and Supplementary file 1.

claim: MCR-MOR expression was associated with small changes in susceptibility to AMPs compared to MCR-1.
source: In general, MCR-MOR expression was associated with small changes in susceptibility to AMPs compared to MCR-1 (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: MCR-MOR expression provided a small increase (5.9-fold) in colistin resistance compared to MCR-1 (13.2-fold).
source: In line with previous work, MCR-MOR expression provided a small increase (5.9-fold) in colistin resistance compared to MCR-1 (13.2-fold) (Wei et al., 2018; AbuOun et al., 2017; Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and citations to two published works (Wei et al., 2018; AbuOun et al., 2017).

claim: MCR-1 and MCR-MOR have similar effects on cell surface charge.
source: However, MCR-1 and MCR-MOR have similar effects on cell surface charge (Figure 3b, p=0.470, two-sided Mann–Whitney U-test), supporting the idea that MCR-1-mediated colistin resistance is also attributable to other factors, such as the increased protection of the cytoplasmic membrane from colisitin (Sabnis et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (p=0.470, two-sided Mann–Whitney U-test) shown in Figure 3b.

claim: MCR-1-mediated colistin resistance is also attributable to other factors, such as the increased protection of the cytoplasmic membrane from colistin.
source: However, MCR-1 and MCR-MOR have similar effects on cell surface charge (Figure 3b, p=0.470, two-sided Mann–Whitney U-test), supporting the idea that MCR-1-mediated colistin resistance is also attributable to other factors, such as the increased protection of the cytoplasmic membrane from colisitin (Sabnis et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and supported by a citation to Sabnis et al., 2021.

claim: MCR-MOR does not confer broad resistance to host AMPs.
source: Given that MCR-MOR does not confer broad resistance to host AMPs, our results suggest that MCR-1 was able to evolve to increase resistance to both colistin and relevant host AMPs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing MCR-1 and MCR-MOR.

claim: MCR-1 was able to evolve to increase resistance to both colistin and relevant host AMPs.
source: Given that MCR-MOR does not confer broad resistance to host AMPs, our results suggest that MCR-1 was able to evolve to increase resistance to both colistin and relevant host AMPs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing MCR-1 and MCR-MOR.

claim: MCR plasmids conferred high levels of resistance to human serum.
source: Interestingly, these MCR plasmids conferred high levels of resistance to human serum, showing that MCR-1 is effective at providing protection against even complex mixtures of antimicrobials (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: MCR-1 is effective at providing protection against even complex mixtures of antimicrobials.
source: Interestingly, these MCR plasmids conferred high levels of resistance to human serum, showing that MCR-1 is effective at providing protection against even complex mixtures of antimicrobials (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: There was no difference in serum resistance between wild-type (carrying no plasmid) and strain with MCR-1 knockout plasmid.
source: We found no difference in serum resistance between wild-type (carrying no plasmid) and strain with MCR-1 knockout plasmid, suggesting that indeed the observed serum resistance phenotype was due to MCR-1 (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The observed serum resistance phenotype was due to MCR-1.
source: We found no difference in serum resistance between wild-type (carrying no plasmid) and strain with MCR-1 knockout plasmid, suggesting that indeed the observed serum resistance phenotype was due to MCR-1 (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Heat inactivation clearly reduced the toxicity of serum to the WT control strain, highlighting the antibacterial effects of heat labile components of serum.
source: Heat inactivation clearly reduced the toxicity of serum to the WT control strain, highlighting the antibacterial effects of heat labile components of serum.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on heat-inactivated serum.

claim: All the tested strains showed similar levels of sensitivity to heat-inactivated serum.
source: All the tested strains showed similar levels of sensitivity to heat-inactivated serum, suggesting that MCR-1-mediated protection against serum (i.e., Figure 4a and b) is due to increased resistance to heat-labile effectors that are present in serum.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on heat-inactivated serum.

claim: MCR-1-mediated protection against serum is due to increased resistance to heat-labile effectors that are present in serum.
source: All the tested strains showed similar levels of sensitivity to heat-inactivated serum, suggesting that MCR-1-mediated protection against serum (i.e., Figure 4a and b) is due to increased resistance to heat-labile effectors that are present in serum.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on heat-inactivated serum.

claim: The presence of functional MCR-1 was not associated with increased resistance to C6-deficient serum.
source: The presence of functional MCR-1 was not associated with increased resistance to C6-defficient serum, providing further evidence to support the role that MCR-1 protects against the complement system.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on C6-deficient serum.

claim: MCR-1 protects against the complement system.
source: The presence of functional MCR-1 was not associated with increased resistance to C6-defficient serum, providing further evidence to support the role that MCR-1 protects against the complement system.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on C6-deficient serum.

claim: AMP resistance in pathogens has been shown to be an important virulence factor.
source: This is plausible as AMP resistance in pathogens has been shown to be an important virulence factor (Groisman et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Groisman et al., 1992.

claim: Previous work has shown that MCR-1 plasmids actually decrease virulence in a G. mellonella model.
source: In contrast to this expectation, previous work has shown that MCR-1 plasmids actually decrease virulence in a G. mellonella model (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: Plasmids with identical mcr-1 genes had differential effects on virulence.
source: However, this study also showed that plasmids with identical mcr-1 genes had differential effects on virulence, suggesting that these plasmids had effects on virulence that were unrelated to MCR-1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from previous work mentioned in the text.

claim: The MCR-1 carrying strain showed increased virulence compared to the control strain with an empty vector in spite of the cost associated with MCR-1 expression.
source: Crucially, the MCR-1 carrying strain showed increased virulence compared to the control strain with an empty vector in spite of the cost associated with MCR-1 expression (Figure 4e, log-rank test, p=0.024, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (log-rank test, p=0.024) shown in Figure 4e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MCR-1-mediated modification of LPS can result in reduced stimulation of macrophages and limited release of inflammatory molecules.
source: MCR-1-mediated modification of LPS can result in reduced stimulation of macrophages and limited release of inflammatory molecules, suggesting that MCR-1 could increase virulence by reducing host immunostimulation (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: MCR-1 continued to increase virulence in LPS-treated larvae.
source: However, MCR-1 continued to increase virulence in LPS-treated larvae, suggesting that reduced host immunostimulation was not responsible for the increased virulence associated with MCR-1 expression (Figure 4f, log-rank test p=0.0074).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (log-rank test p=0.0074) shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Reduced host immunostimulation was not responsible for the increased virulence associated with MCR-1 expression.
source: However, MCR-1 continued to increase virulence in LPS-treated larvae, suggesting that reduced host immunostimulation was not responsible for the increased virulence associated with MCR-1 expression (Figure 4f, log-rank test p=0.0074).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: MCR increases bacterial fitness and resistance in the presence of AMPs from humans and agricultural animals that act as important sources of MCR carrying E. coli.
source: Our study shows that MCR increases bacterial fitness and resistance in the presence of AMPs from humans and agricultural animals that act as important sources of MCR carrying E. coli (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: MCR-1 also increases resistance to human serum and virulence in an insect infection model.
source: MCR-1 also increases resistance to human serum and virulence in an insect infection model, highlighting the threat of infections caused by MCR-E. coli (Yin et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Yin et al., 2021.

claim: MCR-1 provides effective resistance against AMP cocktails that are found in host tissues.
source: These findings suggest that MCR-1 provides effective resistance against AMP cocktails that are found in host tissues, but it is important to emphasize that MCR-mediated protection against other antimicrobials, such as lysozyme (Sherman et al., 2016) and complement systems (Figure 4), may also contribute to this protective phenotype.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: MCR-mediated protection against other antimicrobials, such as lysozyme and complement systems, may also contribute to this protective phenotype.
source: These findings suggest that MCR-1 provides effective resistance against AMP cocktails that are found in host tissues, but it is important to emphasize that MCR-mediated protection against other antimicrobials, such as lysozyme (Sherman et al., 2016) and complement systems (Figure 4), may also contribute to this protective phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sherman et al., 2016 and reference to Figure 4.

claim: The increases in resistance to host AMPs associated with MCR are very modest (typically less than threefold increase).
source: The increases in resistance to host AMPs associated with MCR are very modest (typically less than threefold increase) when viewed from an antibiotic resistance perspective.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: AMP resistance genes typically confer small changes in resistance.
source: However, these subtle and quantitative changes are entirely consistent with previous studies showing that AMP resistance genes typically confer small changes in resistance (Kintses et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kintses et al., 2019.

claim: Subtle changes in AMP resistance are associated with clear selective advantages (i.e., >5%) under clinically realistic concentrations of AMPs.
source: Our study shows that subtle changes in AMP resistance are associated with clear selective advantages (i.e., >5%) under clinically realistic concentrations of AMPs (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: There is growing evidence that mutations leading to small changes in resistance are selected in antibiotic-treated patients.
source: Moreover, there is growing evidence that mutations leading to small changes in resistance are selected in antibiotic-treated patients (Frimodt-Møller et al., 2018; Wheatley et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Frimodt-Møller et al., 2018; Wheatley et al., 2021).

claim: Small effect resistance is likely to be particularly important under conditions when multiple resistance mechanisms can be sequentially acquired, generating a high resistance phenotype.
source: Small effect resistance is likely to be particularly important under conditions when multiple resistance mechanisms can be sequentially acquired, generating a high resistance phenotype (Jochumsen et al., 2016; Jangir et al., 2022; Papkou et al., 2020; Hughes and Andersson, 2017; Toprak et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to five published works (Jochumsen et al., 2016; Jangir et al., 2022; Papkou et al., 2020; Hughes and Andersson, 2017; Toprak et al., 2012).

claim: Anthropogenic use of AMPs (e.g., colistin) can inadvertently drive the evolution of resistance to key components of innate immunity.
source: One of the most important insights from this study is that anthropogenic use of AMPs (e.g., colistin) can inadvertently drive the evolution of resistance to key components of innate immunity (Habets and Brockhurst, 2012; Perron et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study findings and supported by citations to two published works (Habets and Brockhurst, 2012; Perron et al., 2006).

claim: Numerous AMPs are currently in clinical trials, including AMPs of human origin.
source: Numerous AMPs are currently in clinical trials, including AMPs of human origin (Mookherjee et al., 2020; Lazzaro et al., 2020), and our results highlight the importance of assessing the impact of evolved resistance to therapeutic AMPs on resistance to host innate immunity and bacterial virulence during preclinical development using sensitive and quantitative assays.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Mookherjee et al., 2020; Lazzaro et al., 2020).

claim: Cross-resistance to host AMPs is likely to be widespread, given that AMPs tend to share broad cellular targets and physicochemical properties.
source: However, we argue that cross-resistance to host AMPs is likely to be widespread, given that AMPs tend to share broad cellular targets and physicochemical properties (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study findings and reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: Mechanisms that have evolved to provide pathogenic bacteria with protection against host AMPs may also help to accelerate the evolution of resistance to therapeutic AMPs.
source: If this is the case, then it is conceivable that mechanisms that have evolved to provide pathogenic bacteria with protection against host AMPs may also help to accelerate the evolution of resistance to therapeutic AMPs (Jangir et al., 2022; Kapel et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and supported by citations to two published works (Jangir et al., 2022; Kapel et al., 2022).

claim: The Chinese government banned the use of colistin as a growth promoter in 2016.
source: The Chinese government banned the use of colistin as a growth promoter in 2016, and this was followed by a decline in the prevalence of MCR in human, agricultural, and environmental samples at a national level, providing strong evidence that colistin use in agriculture was the key driver for MCR-1 (Shen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Shen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).

claim: The ban on colistin as a growth promoter was followed by a decline in the prevalence of MCR in human, agricultural, and environmental samples at a national level.
source: The Chinese government banned the use of colistin as a growth promoter in 2016, and this was followed by a decline in the prevalence of MCR in human, agricultural, and environmental samples at a national level, providing strong evidence that colistin use in agriculture was the key driver for MCR-1 (Shen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Shen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).

claim: Colistin use in agriculture was the key driver for MCR-1.
source: The Chinese government banned the use of colistin as a growth promoter in 2016, and this was followed by a decline in the prevalence of MCR in human, agricultural, and environmental samples at a national level, providing strong evidence that colistin use in agriculture was the key driver for MCR-1 (Shen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed decline after the ban and supported by citations to two published works (Shen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).

claim: The fitness costs associated with MCR-1 are likely to have played an important role in the decline of colistin resistance.
source: The fitness costs associated with MCR-1 (Yang et al., 2017) are likely to have played an important role in the decline of colistin resistance, but our findings suggest that AMPs from humans and agricultural animals provide a selective advantage for MCR-1 that has helped to offset the cost of colistin resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on inference and supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: AMPs from humans and agricultural animals provide a selective advantage for MCR-1 that has helped to offset the cost of colistin resistance.
